source_refs.note: Chapter 18 exercise (PDF 133-136, printed 129-132), solved: 11 MCQs with keys worked out from the chapter (the book prints no key), model answers to 10 short, 10 constructed and 5 comprehensive questions, and 10 numericals worked step by step.

blocks.prompt: 18.1 Which particle is emitted when UV light is made incident on a zinc surface?
blocks.explanation: UV light has a frequency above the threshold frequency of zinc, so each photon absorbed by an electron of the metal can eject it. This is the photoelectric effect, and the emitted particles are electrons (photoelectrons).

blocks.prompt: 18.2 The wave nature of electrons is supported by experiments on:
blocks.explanation: Diffraction is a wave property. Davisson and Germer showed that electrons are diffracted by a nickel crystal exactly like X-rays, with the wavelength λ = h/mv predicted by de Broglie. The photoelectric effect shows the particle nature of light.

blocks.prompt: 18.3 The dimensions of Planck's constant are same as that of:
blocks.explanation: h = E/f, unit J s = kg m² s⁻¹, dimensions [ML²T⁻¹]. Angular momentum L = mvr also has unit kg m² s⁻¹ (J s). Momentum is kg m s⁻¹ and torque is N m = kg m² s⁻².

blocks.prompt: 18.4 Which of the following has the most energetic photons?
blocks.explanation: Photon energy E = hf. Gamma rays have the highest frequency (shortest wavelength) of these radiations, so their photons have the most energy.

blocks.prompt: 18.5 de-Broglie waves are associated with:

options.text: all particles whether in motion or at rest

blocks.explanation: λ = h/mv applies to every material particle in motion, charged (electrons, protons) or neutral (neutrons, atoms). For a particle at rest, v = 0 and no wavelength is defined.

blocks.prompt: 18.6 An electron microscope employ the principle:

options.text: electron can be focused by an electric field
electron can be focused by a magnetic field

blocks.explanation: An electron microscope uses the wave nature of electrons (very short de Broglie wavelength, so high resolution), and the electron beam is focused by lenses made of fields: electromagnetic (magnetic) lenses, and electric (electrostatic) lenses in some microscopes. So all three principles are used.

blocks.prompt: 18.7 Electron, proton, neutron and alpha particle, all have the same speed, which particle will have the shortest wavelength?
blocks.explanation: λ = h/mv. At the same speed, λ ∝ 1/m, so the heaviest particle has the shortest wavelength. The alpha particle (2 protons + 2 neutrons) is about four times heavier than a proton.

blocks.prompt: 18.8 The Balmer series is obtained when all the transitions of electrons terminate at:
blocks.explanation: Balmer series: 1/λ = R_H(1/2² − 1/n²), n = 3, 4, 5, ... All transitions end on n = 2 (Lyman ends on n = 1, Paschen on n = 3).

blocks.prompt: 18.9 The spectrum in which different colours are not diffused into each other and are separated by dark spaces is usually known as:
blocks.explanation: A line spectrum consists of sharp, separate bright lines (colours) on a dark background, as seen from the vapours of elements in a discharge tube. In a continuous spectrum the colours merge into each other.

blocks.prompt: 18.10 Using uncertainty principle, it can be proved that:

options.text: electron lies out of the nucleus
there is always uncertainty in measuring accurately energy and momentum for atomic particles

blocks.explanation: The chapter uses Δx Δp ≈ h to prove that electrons are not present inside the nucleus: with Δx ≈ 10⁻¹⁵ m, Δp ≈ 6.63 × 10⁻¹⁹ kg m s⁻¹, which needs an energy of the order of GeV; no such electron is found in atoms, so the electron lies outside the nucleus. Option (d) is not a result proved by the principle; the principle itself is about position-momentum (and energy-time), not energy and momentum together.

blocks.prompt: 18.11 According to uncertainty principle, in order to observe the position of an electron with greater accuracy, we must use light of:
blocks.explanation: The position can be found only to within about one wavelength of the light used (Δx ≈ λ). A shorter wavelength gives a smaller Δx, but its photon has a larger momentum h/λ, so the momentum becomes more uncertain.

blocks.prompt: 18.1 How energy of a pocket is related to its frequency according to quantum theory? Describe briefly.
blocks.explanation:
According to quantum theory, radiation is emitted or absorbed in discrete packets of energy (quanta or photons). The energy of each packet is directly proportional to its frequency:
E = hf
where h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s is Planck's constant. Higher frequency means a more energetic packet.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The question prints "pocket"; it means "packet" (a packet of energy, a quantum).

blocks.prompt: 18.2 How does the photoelectric current vary with intensity of incident light on a metal surface?
blocks.explanation: For light above the threshold frequency, the photoelectric current is directly proportional to the intensity of the light. A more intense beam has more photons, so more electrons are ejected per second. The stopping potential (maximum K.E.) does not change with intensity. Below the threshold frequency there is no current, however intense the light.

blocks.prompt: 18.3 Which has more energy, a photon of UV radiation or a photon of yellow light? Describe briefly.
blocks.explanation:
A photon of UV radiation. Photon energy E = hf = hc/λ, and UV has a higher frequency (shorter wavelength) than yellow light.
Example: yellow light (577 nm): E = hc/λ ≈ 3.4 × 10⁻¹⁹ J ≈ 2.2 eV; UV (300 nm): E ≈ 6.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J ≈ 4.1 eV.

blocks.prompt: 18.4 Is work function of a metal related to threshold frequency in a photoelectric emission?
blocks.explanation:
Yes. The work function is the minimum energy needed to free an electron from the metal; a photon of the threshold frequency f₀ has just this energy (K.E.max = 0):
φ = hf₀
So a metal with a larger work function has a higher threshold frequency.

blocks.prompt: 18.5 Explain briefly, why we can observe the wave-like properties of electrons but not of a flying tennis ball.
blocks.explanation: de Broglie wavelength λ = h/mv. An electron has a very small mass, so its wavelength (about 10⁻¹⁰ m) is comparable to the spacing of atoms in a crystal, and its diffraction can be observed. A tennis ball has a large mass, so its wavelength is extremely small (e.g. 0.06 kg at 30 m s⁻¹: λ ≈ 3.7 × 10⁻³⁴ m), far too small to produce any detectable diffraction or interference.

blocks.prompt: 18.6 Radiation with a certain frequency causes electrons to be emitted from the surface of one metal and not from the surface of another metal. Why?
blocks.explanation: Different metals have different work functions, hence different threshold frequencies (φ = hf₀). The radiation's frequency is above the threshold frequency of the first metal (hf > φ₁), so electrons are emitted; it is below the threshold frequency of the second metal (hf < φ₂), so no electrons are emitted, however intense the radiation.

blocks.prompt: 18.7 Will high frequency light has more number of electrons than a low frequency light? Describe briefly.
blocks.explanation: No. The number of photoelectrons emitted depends on the intensity of light (the number of photons per second), not on its frequency, provided the frequency is above the threshold frequency. A higher frequency only increases the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons: K.E.max = hf − φ. (At constant intensity, light of different frequencies gives the same current; Fig. 18.3.)

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: As printed ("Will high frequency light has more number of electrons"), the question reads as if light carries electrons. It means: "Will high frequency light eject a larger number of electrons than low frequency light?" (and "has" should be "have").

blocks.prompt: 18.8 When does light behave as a wave and when does it behaves as consisted of particles?
blocks.explanation: Light behaves as a wave while travelling from the source to the place where it is detected: interference, diffraction and polarization show this. It behaves as a stream of particles (photons) when it interacts with matter: photoelectric effect, Compton effect and pair production show this. Both aspects never appear together in one experiment (principle of complementarity).

blocks.prompt: 18.9 Name two possible spectral line series in the spectrum of atomic hydrogen. In which region of electromagnetic spectrum each lies?
blocks.explanation:
1. Lyman series (transitions ending on n = 1): ultraviolet region.
2. Balmer series (transitions ending on n = 2): visible region.
(Also: Paschen series, transitions ending on n = 3: infrared region.)

blocks.prompt: 18.10 What is meant by shift, and on witch factors does it depend?
blocks.explanation:
Compton shift is the increase in wavelength of X-rays scattered by electrons: Δλ = λ′ − λ.
Δλ = (h/m₀c)(1 − cos θ)
It depends only on the scattering angle θ (zero at θ = 0°, h/m₀c = 2.43 × 10⁻¹² m at 90°, maximum at 180°) and on the rest mass m₀ of the scattering particle; it does not depend on the incident wavelength.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The question prints "witch"; it means "which". "Shift" here is the Compton shift (Section 18.3).

blocks.prompt: 18.1 Why do solids give rise to a continuous spectrum while hot vapours emit line spectrum?
blocks.explanation:
Hot vapours (gas at low pressure): the atoms are far apart and practically isolated, so each atom keeps its own discrete energy levels. Electrons jump only between these levels and emit photons of only certain energies hf = E₂ − E₁, giving separate sharp lines: a line spectrum.
Hot solids: the atoms are closely packed and interact strongly, so their energy levels are disturbed and spread into a very large number of closely spaced levels (bands). Transitions of almost every energy are possible, so all wavelengths are emitted and the colours merge: a continuous spectrum. (The band picture of solids is beyond the chapter.)

blocks.prompt: 18.2 Light can emit electrons from a metal surface and light can also be diffracted. Comment on the statement.
blocks.explanation:
The statement is correct; it shows the dual nature of light.
1. Emission of electrons (photoelectric effect) can only be explained if light consists of photons, each of energy hf, absorbed by single electrons: particle nature.
2. Diffraction (and interference) can only be explained if light is a wave: wave nature.
So light has both natures (wave-particle duality). According to the principle of complementarity, both aspects are needed for its full description, but a single experiment shows only one of them: light travels as a wave and interacts with matter as particles.

blocks.prompt: 18.3 Why X-rays have different properties form light even though both originate from the transition of elections between different energy levels in excited atoms? Describe briefly.
blocks.explanation:
The energy of the photon equals the energy difference of the transition: hf = E_upper − E_lower.
1. Light (visible) comes from transitions of outer electrons, where the energy levels differ by only a few eV, so the photons have low energy, low frequency and long wavelength (about 400–700 nm).
2. X-rays come from transitions of inner electrons (inner shells, such as K and L) of heavy atoms, where the energy differences are thousands of eV (keV). So X-ray photons have very high energy and frequency and very short wavelength (about 10⁻¹⁰ m and less).
Because of their high photon energy, X-rays are highly penetrating and ionizing, unlike light. (X-ray production from inner shells is beyond the chapter.)

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The question prints "form light" and "elections"; they mean "from light" and "electrons".

blocks.prompt: 18.4 Is energy conserved when an atom emits a photon of light? Describe how.
blocks.explanation:
Yes. An excited atom emits a photon when its electron falls from a higher level Eₙ to a lower level Eₚ. The atom loses exactly the energy the photon carries away:
hf = Eₙ − Eₚ
So the total energy (atom + photon) before and after emission is the same. That is why each line has a fixed frequency: f = (Eₙ − Eₚ)/h. (The tiny recoil energy of the atom is negligible.)

blocks.prompt: 18.5 How can spectrum of hydrogen atom contains many spectral lines when hydrogen atom contains one electron only?
blocks.explanation: A sample of hydrogen gas contains an enormous number of atoms. In a discharge, different atoms are excited to different levels (n = 2, 3, 4, ...), and their electrons return to lower levels by different transitions, either directly or in steps (e.g. 3 → 2, 4 → 2, 2 → 1, 3 → 1, 4 → 3). Each kind of transition emits photons of one definite wavelength, hf = Eₙ − Eₚ, giving one line. Since all these transitions take place at the same time in different atoms, the spectrum shows many lines, grouped into series (Lyman, Balmer, Paschen).

blocks.prompt: 18.6 What should be the speed of an electron if it is to be confined in a box of the size of a nucleus?
blocks.explanation:
Size of nucleus: Δx ≈ 10⁻¹⁵ m. By the uncertainty principle:
Δp ≈ h/Δx = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)/(10⁻¹⁵ m) = 6.63 × 10⁻¹⁹ kg m s⁻¹
Δv = Δp/m = (6.63 × 10⁻¹⁹)/(9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg) ≈ 7.3 × 10¹¹ m s⁻¹
This is more than the speed of light (3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹), which is impossible. Treated correctly (relativistically) the electron would have to move at practically the speed of light with energy of the order of GeV (E ≈ pc ≈ 2 × 10⁻¹⁰ J ≈ 1.2 GeV). No electron with such energy is found in atoms, so an electron cannot be confined in a nucleus.

blocks.prompt: 18.7 An incident X-ray on a metal surface is scattered. What is the wavelength, frequency, energy and speed of the scattered X-ray as compared to incident X-ray?
blocks.explanation:
In Compton scattering the photon gives part of its energy to the recoiling electron, so the scattered X-ray has a longer wavelength, a lower frequency and a lower energy than the incident X-ray; its speed is the same (c):
λ′ = λ + (h/m₀c)(1 − cos θ)

rows: Lower: hf′ = hf − K.E. of the recoil electron

blocks.prompt: 18.8 Why does energy and momentum conservation play a key role in driving Compton's effect?
blocks.explanation:
Compton treated the scattering as an elastic collision between an X-ray photon (energy hc/λ, momentum h/λ) and an electron at rest, like two billiard balls.
1. Conservation of energy: hc/λ − hc/λ′ = (m − m₀)c² (the photon's lost energy becomes the electron's K.E.).
2. Conservation of momentum, x-component: h/λ = (h/λ′) cos θ + mv cos φ; y-component: 0 = (h/λ′) sin θ − mv sin φ.
Solving these equations gives the Compton shift Δλ = (h/m₀c)(1 − cos θ), in complete agreement with experiment. Classical wave theory cannot explain the shift, so the success of these conservation laws proves that a photon carries momentum and behaves like a particle.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The question prints "driving"; it means "deriving" (deriving the Compton shift), and "does" should be "do".

blocks.prompt: 18.9 Describe how a line emission spectrum leads to an understanding of the existence of discrete electron energy levels in atoms.
blocks.explanation:
1. The emission spectrum of an element (e.g. hydrogen in a discharge tube) is not continuous; it consists of sharp lines of only certain definite wavelengths.
2. Each line is produced by photons of one energy: hf = hc/λ = Eₙ − Eₚ, the difference between two energy levels.
3. If the electron could have any energy, every energy difference would be possible and a continuous spectrum would appear. Since only certain wavelengths appear, the electron can have only certain discrete energies.
4. The wavelengths follow simple formulas with whole numbers, e.g. Balmer: 1/λ = R_H(1/2² − 1/n²), n = 3, 4, 5, ...; the integers n label the allowed energy levels (n = 1 ground state, n = 2, 3, ... excited states).
5. Absorption lines appear at the same wavelengths, confirming the same fixed levels.

blocks.prompt: 18.10 Mass of a photon is considered zero, then how does the photon possess momentum? Describe.
blocks.explanation:
A photon has zero rest mass, but it always moves with speed c and carries energy E = hf. From the theory of relativity, energy is equivalent to mass (E = mc²), so a moving photon has a mass equivalent m = E/c² and a momentum p = mc:
E = pc, so p = E/c = hf/c = h/λ
Thus the photon's momentum comes from its energy, not from a rest mass. The Compton effect proves it: the photon transfers momentum to an electron like a colliding particle.

blocks.prompt: 18.1 Explain photoelectric effect, its experimental arrangements and observations. Deduce photoelectric equation; hf = φ + 1/2 mv²max.
blocks.explanation:
Photoelectric effect: the emission of electrons from a metal surface when light of suitable frequency (or wavelength) falls on it. The emitted electrons are called photoelectrons.
Experimental arrangement:
1. An evacuated glass tube contains two electrodes: a metal cathode C (connected to the negative terminal of a battery) and an anode A (connected to the positive terminal), through a potential divider and a micro-ammeter.
2. When monochromatic light of suitable frequency falls on C, electrons are emitted, attracted by A, and the micro-ammeter shows a current (photoelectric current). The current stops when the light is cut off.
3. Reversing the battery makes A negative: the electrons are repelled and the current decreases. At a certain negative potential V₀, the stopping potential, the current becomes zero; even the fastest electrons cannot reach A. So (K.E.)max = ½mv²max = V₀e.
Observations:
1. With higher intensity (same frequency) the current increases but stops at the same V₀ (Fig. 18.2): intensity decides only the number of electrons.
2. With constant intensity and different frequencies, the current is the same but V₀ is different (Fig. 18.3): (K.E.)max increases with frequency.
3. Electrons are emitted with different energies; (K.E.)max depends on the metal and the frequency.
4. There is a threshold frequency f₀ (different for each metal) below which no electrons are emitted, however intense the light (e.g. blue light ejects electrons from sodium, red light does not).
5. Emission is instantaneous.
The wave theory cannot explain these results (it predicts K.E. increasing with intensity, no threshold, and a time delay).
Deduction of the photoelectric equation (Einstein):
1. Light consists of photons, each of energy E = hf.
2. A photon is absorbed by a single electron of the metal. A minimum energy φ (work function) is needed for the electron to escape.
3. Part of the photon energy is used to escape and the rest appears as kinetic energy; for electrons coming straight out this is the maximum:
Incident photon energy − work function = (K.E.)max
hf − φ = ½mv²max
hf = φ + ½mv²max
4. At threshold, (K.E.)max = 0 and f = f₀: φ = hf₀. So (K.E.)max = hf − hf₀ = V₀e.
The graph of (K.E.)max against f is a straight line with slope h, cutting the frequency axis at f₀. The photoelectric effect shows the particle nature of light.

blocks.prompt: 18.2 Describe de-Broglie waves associated with material particles and discuss wave particle duality.
blocks.explanation:
de Broglie waves:
1. Light shows a dual nature. Assuming symmetry in nature, Louis de Broglie (1924) proposed that material particles should also have wave properties.
2. The momentum of a photon is p = h/λ. He suggested the same relation for a particle of mass m moving with velocity v:
p = mv = h/λ, so λ = h/p = h/mv (de Broglie relation)
3. For large objects λ is negligibly small: a 20 g bullet at 330 m s⁻¹ has λ ≈ 1 × 10⁻³⁴ m, undetectable. For an electron at 1 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹, λ ≈ 7 × 10⁻¹⁰ m, in the X-ray range, so its diffraction is measurable.
4. Experimental proof (Davisson and Germer): electrons from a heated filament, accelerated through V, are made incident on a nickel crystal; the scattered electrons come off in regular peaks, a diffraction pattern like X-rays. With ½mv² = Ve, mv = √(2mVe) and λ = h/√(2mVe). For V = 54 V, λ = 1.66 × 10⁻¹⁰ m; Bragg's law 2d sin θ = mλ with d = 0.91 × 10⁻¹⁰ m and θ = 65° gives λ = 1.65 × 10⁻¹⁰ m, in excellent agreement. Diffraction has also been observed with protons, neutrons and hydrogen and helium atoms.
Wave-particle duality:
1. Light: interference and diffraction show its wave nature; the photoelectric and Compton effects show its particle nature.
2. Matter: electron diffraction (Davisson-Germer, G. P. Thomson) shows the wave nature of electrons; J. J. Thomson's e/m experiment treats them as particles.
3. So matter and radiation both have a dual wave-particle nature. Bohr's principle of complementarity: both aspects are needed for a complete description, but both are never revealed in a single experiment; the experiment decides which aspect appears (a grating reveals light as a wave, a metal surface as particles).
4. All micro-particles propagate as waves and exchange energy as particles.

blocks.prompt: 18.3 Explain the appearance and formation of emission and absorption of line spectra from excited atoms. How can they be used to identify the presence of varies elements in a mixture of vapours?
blocks.explanation:
Emission line spectrum:
1. Arrangement: light from a discharge tube containing a gas or vapour is passed through a spectrometer with a diffraction grating.
2. Appearance: a series of sharp bright lines of definite wavelengths is seen on a dark background.
3. Formation: in the discharge, atoms absorb energy and their electrons are raised to higher (excited) levels. Excited states have a very short life; the electrons return to lower levels and emit photons of energy hf = Eₙ − Eₚ. Only certain energy differences exist, so only certain wavelengths (lines) appear. For hydrogen: Lyman series (ends on n = 1, ultraviolet), Balmer series 1/λ = R_H(1/2² − 1/n²) (ends on n = 2, visible), Paschen series (ends on n = 3, infrared).
Absorption line spectrum:
1. Appearance: when white light (a continuous spectrum) is passed through a gas at low pressure, dark lines appear in the continuous spectrum at certain wavelengths.
2. Formation: the electrons of the gas atoms absorb only photons whose energy exactly equals an upward transition, Eₙ − Eₚ. These wavelengths are removed from the light (they are re-emitted in all directions), so dark lines are left in their places.
3. The wavelengths missing in the absorption spectrum are exactly those present in the emission spectrum of the same element (Fig. 18.13).
Identification of elements in a mixture:
1. Every element has its own set of energy levels, so its line spectrum is unique, like a fingerprint.
2. The spectrum of the excited mixture of vapours (or the absorption spectrum of light passed through it) is recorded, and the wavelengths of its lines are measured.
3. The lines are compared with the known spectra of elements. If all the characteristic lines of an element are present, that element is present in the mixture (e.g. the two yellow lines near 589 nm show sodium). The brightness of the lines also gives an idea of the amount.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The question prints "varies elements"; it means "various elements".

blocks.prompt: 18.4 Describe the transmission of electron microscope. What are the similarities and differences between electron microscope and an optical microscope?
blocks.explanation:
Transmission electron microscope (TEM):
1. Principle: it uses the wave nature of electrons. Fast electrons have a de Broglie wavelength thousands of times shorter than visible light, so the microscope can show much finer details (down to nanometre, near atomic, level). The higher the speed of the electrons, the shorter the wavelength and the higher the resolution.
2. Source: electrons from a heated filament (electron gun) are accelerated by a very high voltage, in vacuum.
3. Condenser lens: an electromagnetic lens focuses the beam on a thin specimen. The electrons pass (are transmitted) through the specimen.
4. Objective lens: an electromagnetic lens forms an image of the specimen.
5. Projector lens: an electromagnetic lens further magnifies the image and projects it onto a fluorescent screen or a photographic film; the photograph is called a micrograph.
(Modern scanning electron microscopes give three-dimensional images.) Uses: study of cells, viruses and bacteria, metal fractures, materials and crystal structure.
Similarities: both form a magnified image of an object; both use a condenser to focus the beam on the specimen, an objective to form the image and a further lens (projector or eyepiece) to magnify it; in both, the resolution is limited by the wavelength of the wave used.
Differences are given in the table.

rows: Uses a beam of electrons (matter waves)
Wavelength thousands of times shorter than light
Very high resolution: details down to nanometre (near atomic) level
Lower resolution: cannot show details smaller than about the wavelength of light
Electromagnetic (magnetic) lenses; focus changed by changing the current
Glass lenses; focus changed by moving the lenses
Works in vacuum; very high accelerating voltage needed
Works in air; no high voltage needed
Image seen on a fluorescent screen or photographed (micrograph)
Image seen directly by the eye

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The question prints "the transmission of electron microscope"; it means "the transmission electron microscope" (the TEM of Fig. 18.8).

blocks.prompt: 18.5 State and explain uncertainty principle. What is its significance in particle physics?
blocks.explanation:
Statement (Heisenberg, 1927): the position and momentum of a particle cannot both be measured simultaneously with perfect accuracy. The product of the uncertainty Δx in position and the uncertainty Δp in the x-component of momentum at the same instant is approximately equal to Planck's constant:
Δx Δp ≈ h
Explanation:
1. The uncertainty is not due to the instrument; it is a consequence of the wave-particle duality of matter and radiation.
2. To locate a micro-particle we must use light of wavelength λ. Because light is a wave, the position is known only to within about one wavelength: Δx ≈ λ.
3. The photon used has momentum h/λ and may transfer all of it to the particle, so the particle's momentum becomes uncertain by Δp ≈ h/λ.
4. Multiplying: Δx Δp ≈ λ(h/λ) ≈ h.
5. Shorter wavelength gives a smaller Δx but a larger Δp, and vice versa: we cannot reduce both.
6. Heisenberg's more careful calculation gives at best Δx Δp ≥ ħ, where ħ = h/2π = 1.05 × 10⁻³⁴ J s.
7. Energy-time form: ΔE Δt ≈ h (ΔE Δt ≥ ħ). The more accurately the energy is known, the more uncertain the time during which the particle has that energy.
8. For macroscopic objects the uncertainty is negligible (photons hardly affect a flying tennis ball), but in the atomic domain it is dominant (one photon drastically changes an electron's motion).
Significance in particle physics:
1. It proves that electrons cannot exist inside the nucleus: Δx ≈ 10⁻¹⁵ m gives Δp ≈ 6.63 × 10⁻¹⁹ kg m s⁻¹, requiring energy of the order of GeV, which no electron in an atom has.
2. It explains the natural width of spectral lines: an excited state living about 10⁻⁸ s has ΔE ≈ h/Δt ≈ 4 × 10⁻⁷ eV.
3. It sets the fundamental limit of measurement in the atomic world, so the motion of micro-particles is described by probabilities, not exact paths; few things can be predicted with 100% precision.
4. It explains why short wavelengths (high-energy particles or photons) are needed to probe very small structures.

blocks.prompt: 18.1 A photon has wavelength 350 nm. What is its energy in joules and also in eV? (Ans: 5.68 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, 3.55 eV)
blocks.explanation:
Given: λ = 350 nm = 350 × 10⁻⁹ m, h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹
Required: E in J and in eV
E = hf = hc/λ
E = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s × 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)/(350 × 10⁻⁹ m)
E = 5.68 × 10⁻¹⁹ J
As 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J:
E = (5.68 × 10⁻¹⁹)/(1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹) eV = 3.55 eV
Answer: E = 5.68 × 10⁻¹⁹ J = 3.55 eV (agrees with the book).

blocks.prompt: 18.2 A certain atom has a separation in energy of 3 × 10⁻¹⁸ J between two of its energy levels. What frequency photon is required to make the atom change from the lower state to higher state? (Ans: 4.5 × 10¹⁴ Hz)
blocks.explanation:
Given: ΔE = 3 × 10⁻¹⁸ J, h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s
Required: f
The photon must have energy equal to the separation: hf = ΔE
f = ΔE/h
f = (3 × 10⁻¹⁸ J)/(6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)
f = 4.52 × 10¹⁵ Hz ≈ 4.5 × 10¹⁵ Hz
Answer: f = 4.5 × 10¹⁵ Hz (the book prints 4.5 × 10¹⁴ Hz; see the box).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints 4.5 × 10¹⁴ Hz. f = ΔE/h = (3 × 10⁻¹⁸ J)/(6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s) = 4.5 × 10¹⁵ Hz; the power of ten in the printed answer is one too small (it would need ΔE = 3 × 10⁻¹⁹ J).

blocks.prompt: 18.3 What is the wavelength of photon with an energy of 10 × 10⁻¹⁹ J? (124 nm) (Ans: 1.99 × 10⁻⁷ m)
blocks.explanation:
Given: E = 10 × 10⁻¹⁹ J = 1 × 10⁻¹⁸ J, h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹
Required: λ
E = hc/λ, so λ = hc/E
λ = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s × 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)/(1 × 10⁻¹⁸ J)
λ = 1.99 × 10⁻⁷ m = 199 nm
Answer: λ = 1.99 × 10⁻⁷ m (agrees with the book's answer; the "(124 nm)" printed in the question does not; see the box).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The question also prints "(124 nm)", which contradicts the printed answer 1.99 × 10⁻⁷ m (= 199 nm). For E = 10 × 10⁻¹⁹ J the wavelength is 199 nm; 124 nm would be the wavelength of a 10 eV (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁸ J) photon.

blocks.prompt: 18.4 Calculate the threshold frequency for sodium metal whose work function is 2.28 eV and the value of h is 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s. (Ans: 5.5 × 10¹⁴ Hz)
blocks.explanation:
Given: φ = 2.28 eV = 2.28 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J = 3.65 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s
Required: f₀
φ = hf₀, so f₀ = φ/h
f₀ = (3.65 × 10⁻¹⁹ J)/(6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)
f₀ = 5.5 × 10¹⁴ Hz
Answer: f₀ = 5.5 × 10¹⁴ Hz (agrees with the book).

blocks.prompt: 18.5 What can be the longest wavelength for photoelectric emission from tungsten if its work function is 4.54 eV. (Ans: 273 nm)
blocks.explanation:
Given: φ = 4.54 eV = 4.54 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J = 7.26 × 10⁻¹⁹ J
Required: longest (threshold) wavelength λ₀
The longest wavelength corresponds to the threshold frequency: φ = hf₀ = hc/λ₀
λ₀ = hc/φ
λ₀ = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s × 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)/(7.26 × 10⁻¹⁹ J)
λ₀ = 2.74 × 10⁻⁷ m ≈ 274 nm
Answer: λ₀ ≈ 2.7 × 10⁻⁷ m (274 nm with h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹; the book's 273 nm comes from more precise constants, so it agrees).

blocks.prompt: 18.6 An electron is accelerated in an evacuated tube from rest through a potential difference of 550 V. What will be its final momentum? Calculate the wavelength associate with this electron. (Ans: 1.27 × 10⁻²³ N s, 5.22 × 10⁻¹¹ m)
blocks.explanation:
Given: V = 550 V, m = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg, e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, starts from rest
Required: p and λ
K.E. gained: ½mv² = Ve
So mv = √(2mVe)
p = √(2 × 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg × 550 V × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
p = √(1.60 × 10⁻⁴⁶)
p = 1.27 × 10⁻²³ N s (kg m s⁻¹)
de Broglie wavelength: λ = h/p
λ = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)/(1.27 × 10⁻²³ N s)
λ = 5.22 × 10⁻¹¹ m
Answer: p = 1.27 × 10⁻²³ N s, λ = 5.22 × 10⁻¹¹ m (agrees with the book; unrounded p gives 5.24 × 10⁻¹¹ m).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The question prints "associate"; it means "associated" (the wavelength associated with this electron).

blocks.prompt: 18.7 The position of a free electron is determined with an uncertainty of 10⁻⁷ m. What is the uncertainty in its velocity? What would be the position of an electron after one second? (Ans: 6 × 10² m s⁻¹, anywhere within a distance of 6 × 10² m)
blocks.explanation:
Given: Δx = 10⁻⁷ m, m = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg, h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, t = 1 s
Required: Δv, and the position after 1 s
Using the chapter's form Δx Δp ≈ h (as in Example 18.4), with Δp = mΔv:
Δv ≈ h/(mΔx)
Δv ≈ (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)/(9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg × 10⁻⁷ m)
Δv ≈ 7.3 × 10³ m s⁻¹
Position after 1 s: since the velocity is uncertain by Δv, the distance covered in 1 s is uncertain by Δv × t:
Δx′ = Δv × t = 7.3 × 10³ m s⁻¹ × 1 s ≈ 7.3 × 10³ m
So after one second the electron could be anywhere within about 7 × 10³ m.
The book's answer uses the form Δx Δp ≥ h/4π (= ħ/2), not given in the chapter (beyond the chapter):
Δv ≥ h/(4πmΔx) = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴)/(4π × 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ × 10⁻⁷) ≈ 5.8 × 10² m s⁻¹ ≈ 6 × 10² m s⁻¹
and after 1 s: anywhere within 6 × 10² m.
Answer: Δv ≈ 7.3 × 10³ m s⁻¹ and position anywhere within ≈ 7 × 10³ m (with Δx Δp ≈ h); the book's 6 × 10² m s⁻¹ and 6 × 10² m follow from Δx Δp ≥ h/4π (see the box).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed answers (6 × 10² m s⁻¹, 6 × 10² m) do not follow from the chapter's relation Δx Δp ≈ h (Eq. 18.14, used in Example 18.4), which gives Δv ≈ 7.3 × 10³ m s⁻¹ and about 7 × 10³ m. They follow from the stricter form Δx Δp ≥ h/4π (ħ/2), which the chapter does not give. Both workings are shown above.

blocks.prompt:
18.8 A stationary nickel nucleus of mass 9.95 × 10⁻²⁶ kg emits a photon of energy 1.17 MeV. Find:
(i) the wavelength of the photon and its momentum.
(ii) the speed of the nucleus after the emission of photon.
(Ans: (I) 1.06 × 10⁻¹² m, 6.25 × 10⁻²² N s, (ii) 6.29 × 10³ m s⁻¹)
blocks.explanation:
Given: M = 9.95 × 10⁻²⁶ kg (at rest), E = 1.17 MeV = 1.17 × 10⁶ × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J = 1.87 × 10⁻¹³ J
Required: (i) λ and p of the photon, (ii) recoil speed v of the nucleus
(i) E = hc/λ, so λ = hc/E
λ = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s × 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)/(1.87 × 10⁻¹³ J)
λ = 1.06 × 10⁻¹² m
p = h/λ = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)/(1.06 × 10⁻¹² m)
p = 6.25 × 10⁻²² N s
(ii) Conservation of momentum: the nucleus was at rest, so after emission the nucleus and the photon have equal and opposite momenta:
Mv = p
v = p/M = (6.25 × 10⁻²² N s)/(9.95 × 10⁻²⁶ kg)
v = 6.28 × 10³ m s⁻¹ ≈ 6.3 × 10³ m s⁻¹
Answer: (i) λ = 1.06 × 10⁻¹² m, p = 6.25 × 10⁻²² N s; (ii) v ≈ 6.3 × 10³ m s⁻¹ (agrees with the book's 6.29 × 10³ m s⁻¹ within rounding).

blocks.prompt: 18.9 The work function of a metal is 3.5 eV. Light of wavelength 450 nm is incident on the surface. Find out whether electrons will be emitted by the photoelectric effect, from the surface. (Ans: Electrons will not be emitted)
blocks.explanation:
Given: φ = 3.5 eV, λ = 450 nm = 450 × 10⁻⁹ m
Required: is hf ≥ φ?
E = hc/λ
E = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s × 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)/(450 × 10⁻⁹ m)
E = 4.42 × 10⁻¹⁹ J
E = (4.42 × 10⁻¹⁹)/(1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹) eV = 2.76 eV
Since 2.76 eV < 3.5 eV (photon energy less than the work function), no electron can escape.
(Equivalently, threshold wavelength λ₀ = hc/φ = 1.99 × 10⁻²⁵/(5.6 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 355 nm, and 450 nm is longer.)
Answer: Electrons will not be emitted (agrees with the book).

blocks.prompt: 18.10 A 90 keV X-ray photon is fired at a carbon target and Compton scattering occurs. Find the wavelength of the incident photon and the wavelength of the scattered photon for scattering angle of (a) 30° (b) 60°. (Ans: 13.8 pm (a) 14.1 pm (b) 15 pm)
blocks.explanation:
Given: E = 90 keV = 90 × 10³ × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J = 1.44 × 10⁻¹⁴ J, Compton wavelength h/m₀c = 2.43 × 10⁻¹² m = 2.43 pm
Required: λ, and λ′ at θ = 30° and 60°
Incident wavelength: λ = hc/E
λ = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s × 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)/(1.44 × 10⁻¹⁴ J)
λ = 1.38 × 10⁻¹¹ m = 13.8 pm
Compton shift: Δλ = (h/m₀c)(1 − cos θ), λ′ = λ + Δλ
(a) θ = 30°: 1 − cos 30° = 1 − 0.866 = 0.134
Δλ = 2.43 pm × 0.134 = 0.33 pm
λ′ = 13.8 pm + 0.33 pm = 14.1 pm
(b) θ = 60°: 1 − cos 60° = 1 − 0.5 = 0.5
Δλ = 2.43 pm × 0.5 = 1.22 pm
λ′ = 13.8 pm + 1.22 pm = 15.0 pm
Answer: λ = 13.8 pm; (a) λ′ = 14.1 pm; (b) λ′ = 15 pm (agrees with the book).
